title: Binary Search: Find First and Last Position
oneLiner: The same divide-in-half idea, aimed at a BOUNDARY instead of one exact match -- find where a value's range starts and ends.
keyTakeaway: Binary search doesn't require an exact-match target -- it works on any sorted true/false condition ("is nums[i] >= target"), which is why it can find the FIRST or LAST occurrence of a duplicated value just as easily as finding one occurrence: instead of stopping the moment you find a match, keep narrowing toward whichever end of the match-range you're after.
explanation: With duplicates in a sorted array, a plain binary search finds A match, but not necessarily the first or last one. Fix: run the same left/right/mid search, but don't stop on a match -- record it as the best answer so far, then keep searching. To find the FIRST occurrence, keep searching the LEFT half after a match (right = mid - 1); to find the LAST occurrence, keep searching the RIGHT half after a match (left = mid + 1). Run both (a first-search and a last-search) to get the whole range. Watch out for the two failure directions: no match found at all (return [-1, -1]), versus a match found but the OTHER end still needs its own separate search -- finding the first occurrence tells you nothing about where the last one is without actually running the mirrored search.

visualizationSteps.message: Finding the FIRST occurrence of 8. Same binary search, but on a match, don't stop -- keep searching the LEFT half in case there's an earlier one.
nums[3] == 8 -- record index 3 as a candidate, but keep searching left in case there's an earlier one: right = 2.
nums[1]=7 < 8 -- too small, search right. left = 2.
nums[2]=7 < 8 -- too small, search right. left = 3.
Search space exhausted. First occurrence of 8 is at index 3. A mirror-image search (keep going RIGHT on a match instead of left) finds the last occurrence the same way.

recognitionSignals: The array is sorted but has DUPLICATES, and you need the boundary of a run of equal values, not just any one match.
The problem can be reframed as "find the first index where some condition becomes true" (or stops being true) in sorted/monotonic data.
gotchas: Finding one occurrence and assuming it's the first (or last) is wrong with duplicates -- a plain binary search can land anywhere inside the matching run.
The first-search and last-search are mirror images of each other (which side you keep narrowing into after a match) -- easy to copy-paste one and forget to flip the direction for the other.
If the target isn't present at all, both searches need to correctly report "not found" (e.g. -1) rather than returning wherever the search happened to stop.
confusableWith: Binary Search: Find a Target (this track) is the building block -- this lesson is that same search run twice with a small bias added, not a different algorithm.

complexity.note: Two binary searches back to back -- 2·log n is still O(log n).
